Madhuri, you asked how I got Nikhil's parents to visit less without a war. Honestly? I said thank you first. And I meant it.
They'd been coming over three or four evenings a week since the wedding. I was exhausted. But I also remembered how Papaji had run around for weeks arranging the wedding hall, and how Mummyji had stitched my dupatta edges herself at two in the morning.
So one Sunday, I'm Sarita, the one who usually blurts things out, I sat with them and said, "I don't think I ever properly thanked you for the wedding. The hall, the dupatta, all of it. We'd have been lost without you."
Mummyji's eyes filled up.
Then I said, "Because we love having you, I want the visits to be relaxed, not rushed after my long days. Could we do Sundays and one weekday?"
And she said, "Of course, beta. You're tired." That's it.

I'm Lokesh, Amandeep's neighbour; our balconies face each other in Mohali, so I saw more of this than I should admit.
Her in-laws visited nearly every day after the wedding. Some evenings Amandeep looked worn out, smiling at the door but sagging once it closed.
One Sunday, I saw her carry out a tray of tea and a small framed photo of the wedding. She gave the photo to her father-in-law. I could hear her say, "You arranged everything, the band, the langar. I've never thanked you properly."
Her mother-in-law touched her cheek.
Then Amandeep spoke more quietly, and I only caught, "...Saturdays and Wednesdays, so I can give you proper time..."
Her father-in-law nodded. There was no raised voice, no slammed door.
I can't know what she felt, but over the next weeks, the visits were fewer and the laughter on that balcony was louder.

qa.a: A small framed photo of the wedding.

Home-loan officer's note — Sachin and Aparna, first consultation, Pune branch. Written by Chinmay.

Most young couples walk in with a flat already chosen and ask how much we can lend. These two came the other way round.
Sachin had a sheet with their combined monthly take-home pay. Aparna explained their rule: whatever the EMI, it must stay below one-third of that figure, so they can still save and live. They had worked out that maximum EMI before looking at a single flat.
Aparna asked me, "At that EMI, what loan amount does that come to for twenty years?" I worked out an estimate. Sachin added their savings for the down payment and wrote a price ceiling at the bottom of the sheet.
"So we only look at flats under this," he said.
What I did next: I gave them the formal eligibility checklist and suggested they confirm the figures with the bank before booking anything.

qa.a: It must stay below one-third of their combined monthly take-home pay.

qa.a: They seemed calm and confident, having worked out their limit before looking at flats instead of feeling pushed by a loan offer.

Friday night

Suresh and I spent all evening with a calculator instead of watching the film we'd planned. Worth it.
Keerthana at work told me she chose her flat first and then found the EMI ate half her salary. She's stopped going out at all. I don't want that.
So we started from the other end. Our monthly income, both salaries together. We decided the EMI must remain below one-third of that, so there's room for savings, Amma's medicines and an actual life.
Then: what loan does that EMI allow over twenty years? Suresh used the bank's online calculator. Add what we've saved for the down payment. That gave us a top price.
It's lower than the flats on the ads Suresh keeps showing me. That hurt a bit. But now I know which listings to skip.
Next week we're meeting the bank to confirm it properly.
— Vandana

Before the first viewing, Ujjwal and I sat on the steps of our rented building in Hyderabad with one sheet of paper and two columns.
Must-haves: under fifteen minutes' walk to a metro station, because we both commute. A decent school nearby, because we're planning a baby in the next couple of years. Two bedrooms. Within budget.
Nice-to-haves: a balcony, a gym in the complex, an east-facing kitchen, which my mother cares about more than I do.
The first flat we saw had a gorgeous balcony. I fell a little in love. Then Ujjwal quietly asked the agent how far the metro was. Twenty-five minutes by auto. We looked at the sheet and left.
The fifth one had no balcony at all, but was six minutes from the metro and next to a school. We didn't even argue.
— Rukmini

Subject: Our flat plan, version 1

Hi Swati,

After last night's talk, I've put it all in one place so we don't have to remember.
1. Target: the down payment we agreed on, by December two years from now.
2. On the 2nd of every month, the day after both salaries come in, an automatic transfer from each of our accounts into the separate savings account. I've already set mine up. Can you do yours this weekend?
3. A shared sheet with one line per month: amount in, running total, how far we are from the target. I've made the first row.
4. Our yearly bonuses go straight into the account in April. No debate each year; we decided it now.
The point is that we don't have to be disciplined every month. The transfer happens whether we feel like it or not.
If you want to change anything, edit the sheet.

Thomas

Himani, you want to know how we saved for the down payment? No magic. It's because we stopped trusting ourselves.
The first year, Asha and I would say, "This month we'll save a lot." Then there'd be a wedding, or a sale, or my bike would break down, and the month was gone.

Dear Reena didi,

You asked which flat we're choosing. The answer surprised us both.
We were sure it would be the one in Andheri, the one with the lovely lobby. Karan loved it from the first visit. So did I.
But Karan's brother suggested we score all four flats properly. So one evening we made a table. Four things: price, commute, builder's reputation, resale later. We argued for an hour about weights. Then we scored each flat out of ten. Andheri came third. Its commute was awful and the builder has delays on two other projects.
The winner was the plain-looking one in Goregaon. Not exciting. But it scored highest overall.
We're seeing it again on Saturday, with fresh eyes.

Love,
Pooja

Dhruv, you're stuck choosing between flats? Let me tell you what Mark and I did last spring. I'm Elizabeth, and I'm a terrible decision-maker, so this helped.
We had four flats in Kochi on our list. My heart was set on the one near the backwaters. Sunset views. I'd already imagined my plants there.
Mark suggested a spreadsheet. I rolled my eyes, but we did it. Four columns: price, commute, how reliable the builder was, and how easy it would be to sell later. We agreed weights together; commute mattered most for Mark, price mattered most for me, so we met in the middle.
When we added the scores, my backwater flat came last. The builder had a history of late handovers, and it was an hour from Mark's office.
The winner was a boring block near the metro. We live there now. I still miss the sunset idea, honestly. But I don't miss what we avoided.

Sunday night

Eleven months of flat-hunting. Shalini and I were both exhausted, and last night we snapped at each other over a parking space in a flat we hadn't even bought.
Today my brother Lokesh came for lunch and asked, "What exactly are you looking for?" We rattled off the list: near Shalini's office, two bedrooms, a school nearby, a lift, within budget.
"And have you seen flats with all of that?"
"Yes, maybe five."
"Then why are you still looking?"
We had no answer. So we made a rule, right there at the table: from now on, the first flat that meets every must-have and is within budget, we take. No "one more viewing".
Next Saturday we'll go back to the list and look at what's open.
Writing this, I feel lighter than I have in months.
— Yogesh
